summary: Phase 3 of the myidsan productization plan ("Policy"): configurable password strength, optional MFA enforcement, bcrypt-hashed relying-app client secrets, per-account login lockout, and CSRF protection on the server-rendered auth pages. A new passwordPolicy config block (minLength default 12, optional upper/lower/digit/symbol requirements defaulting off, an embedded common-password denylist defaulting on, and a same-as-username rejection) is now enforced at all four paths that ever set a human-chosen password -- self-registration, admin-provisioned account creation (POST /api/user-credential, previously the only path with no strength check at all), authenticated change-password, and the self-service token-based reset -- via a new ValidatePassword funnel; server-generated credentials (the bootstrap/temporary 16-character CSPRNG passwords) are exempt by design, and GET /api/login/password-policy publishes the effective rules for the UI. A new mfa config block (policy: off/optional/required, default optional; requiredRoleIds to narrow required to specific roles; applyToDirectory, default false, to also cover LDAP-bound accounts) adds a shared AccessPrincipal.MustEnrollMfa flag and MfaEnrollmentRequiredCode sentinel, checked by the RBAC middleware after the password gate: a user who owes a factor still gets a session but is pinned to the enrollment screen, never refused outright, so switching the policy on cannot lock out every existing administrator at once. Relying-app client secrets (app_auth_config) move from an unsalted single-round SHA-256 -- a database read used to hand an attacker every operator-chosen client secret at GPU speed -- to bcrypt; the token endpoint accepts both the current and legacy hash form and rewrites a legacy row to bcrypt the first time its secret is presented, so an existing install migrates itself with no operator action. The shared failed-login lockout now keys on both the connecting IP and the submitted account identifier (previously IP-only), closing a gap where a password spray distributed across many source addresses against one account was completely unthrottled; the lockout check moved to after request-body decoding on the affected handlers so the account key is available, and token-based steps (MFA code redemption, the forgot-password request) stay source-keyed only since they present a challenge token or an unproven identifier rather than a password. Finally, the server-rendered /api/auth/{login,mfa,forgot,reset} pages -- public routes that never pass through the session-bound CSRF middleware and previously had none -- gain a session-less double-submit CSRF token (cookie + hidden field, __Host--prefixed over TLS) validated on every POST.
compatibility: All new config blocks are optional and default to safe, low-friction values: an absent passwordPolicy resolves to minLength 12 with composition rules off and the common-password denylist on (up from an inconsistently-enforced hard-coded 8-character minimum on only two of four password paths); an absent or unset mfa block resolves to policy 'optional', identical to today's opt-in-only behavior, so no existing install is pinned to enrollment by this change alone. The per-account login lockout is a deliberate, accepted tradeoff: an attacker who knows a username can now lock that account out by spraying it -- a recoverable nuisance (the window expires, or any successful sign-in clears both counters) traded against the prior unthrottled guessing against a known account. Client secret hashes migrate lazily and transparently: existing legacy-hashed rows keep authenticating and are rewritten to bcrypt the first time each is presented at the token endpoint, with no operator action and no need to re-register any relying app. Operators planning to set mfa.policy to required on a live install should first confirm at least one administrator has an enrolled factor, or is present to enroll immediately after restart -- the RESET_MFA marker file remains the escape hatch for a sole superadmin who gets stuck. No schema changes; all additions are to config.json-level blocks or existing hash/lockout logic.
